# Atlas Research Institute

> Atlas Research Institute supports student research groups worldwide. A research group is three to ten students working one research question, run by a student lead, at a school, in a community setting, hybrid, or fully online. Groups work in any of eight fields. Atlas provides onboarding, research frameworks, mentor feedback at set checkpoints, guest sessions with university researchers, and a route to submit completed work for review. Free.

Atlas Research Institute is a nonprofit. Its primary programme is a network of
student-led research groups. It also runs a separate, selective four-week summer
fellowship; applications for the current fellowship cohort are closed and a
waitlist is open for the next cycle.

Atlas is topic agnostic. A research group investigates a question in its own
local context, in whichever field that question belongs to. Atlas does not
specialise in a single subject area.

## What Atlas Does

- Supports student research groups in eight fields: computer science and AI,
  health and life sciences, engineering and technology, physical sciences and
  mathematics, social sciences, humanities, economics and business, environment
  and sustainability
- Provides onboarding for new groups and session-by-session research frameworks
- Provides mentor guidance and written feedback at set checkpoints
- Runs webinars, workshops, and guest sessions with university researchers
- Reviews weekly logs and research milestones so a stalled project is caught early
- Refers groups to specialised mentorship where a project needs expertise Atlas
  does not hold in-house
- Publishes the Atlas Journal, which accepts completed work for review

## How a Research Group Works

1. A student lead recruits three to ten members and defines one research question.
2. The group meets weekly and keeps a written log of what was done.
3. The project is split into milestones so progress is visible.
4. A mentor reviews the question, the sources, and the draft at set checkpoints.
5. Completed work may be submitted to the Atlas Journal for review.

## Publication

Publication is decided by review. Submission is not acceptance. The Atlas
research and editorial team evaluates submitted work on whether the question is
answerable, the methods are described in enough detail to follow, the sources are
credible and accurately cited, the conclusions match the evidence, and the
limitations are stated honestly. Revision is the normal outcome. Some work is
declined, with reasons given in writing.

The Atlas Journal runs two separate tracks. Atlas Working Papers are founding
contributions from the Atlas team, published without external peer review.
Peer-Reviewed Articles have completed external review; the first reviewed issue
has not yet been published. These two tracks are not equivalent and are not
presented as though they are.

## Who It Is For

- Secondary and university students worldwide, including Grade 8 or below,
  Grades 9 through 12, gap year students, college and university students, and
  international equivalents
- Students who want to run or join a research project in any field
- No prior research experience required
- Free

## The Fellowship

A separate programme from research groups: a selective four-week summer cohort,
free and remote. The current cohort is underway, so applications are closed. The
waitlist is open and next cohort dates are announced to the waitlist first.
Fellows receive research methodology training, structured mentor feedback, guest
sessions with university researchers, a completed literature review or policy
brief, and eligibility to submit completed work for review. A student may both
join a research group and apply to the fellowship.

## Partners

- Submission routes: the Atlas Journal, and the International Journal of High
  School Research
- Programme partners: Lumiere Education, which offers fellows thousands of
  dollars in discounts on Lumiere Education programmes through the partnership;
  The Curieux Review, which partners with Atlas on student research writing
- Fellows learn from researchers at USC, the University of Melbourne, and
  Stanford
